title: Time Passes · 9
paragraphs: The house had been left; the house stood deserted. Now that life had gone out of it, it was left like a shell on a sand dune, to fill up with dry grains of salt. The long night seemed to have begun; the trivial little airs that nibbled, the damp breaths that fumbled, seemed to have won the day. Rust had got into the saucepan, and the mat had rotted. Toads had nosed their way indoors. The shawl swung to and fro, idly, without purpose. In the larder a thistle forced its way up between the tiles. Swallows built nests in the drawing room; straw littered the floor; plaster came down by the shovelful; the beams showed through; rats carried off odds and ends to gnaw behind the wooden paneling. Tortoiseshell butterflies broke out of their chrysalises and beat their lives away against the windowpane. Poppies seeded themselves among the dahlias; long grass waved on the lawn; huge artichokes towered over the roses; a fringed carnation bloomed among the cabbages. And the soft tapping of a weed against the window had turned, on winter nights, into a drumming of sturdy trees and thorny briars, and in summer these made the whole room green.

What power was there now to stop the fertility of nature, its blind indifference? Mrs. McNab’s dream of a lady, a child, a plate of milk soup? That had flickered across the walls like a patch of sunlight and was gone. She had locked the door and left. One woman couldn’t manage it, she said. They never sent word. They never wrote. Up there, things were rotting in the drawers—a shame to leave them like that, she said. The whole place had gone to rack and ruin. Only the beam from the Lighthouse entered the rooms, for a moment at a time, throwing its sudden stare across bed and wall in the winter dark and gazing without concern at the thistle and the swallow, the rat and the straw. There was nothing left to stand against them, nothing to tell them no. So let the wind blow. Let the poppy sow itself, and the carnation mate with the cabbage. Let the swallow nest in the drawing room, the thistle shoulder the tiles aside, the butterfly sun itself on the faded chintz of the armchairs. Let the broken glass and china lie out on the lawn, overgrown and tangled with grass and wild berries.

For the moment had come—that pause when dawn trembles and night holds still, when a single feather dropped into the scale would tip it. One feather, and the house would have sunk and fallen, turning over and pitching down into the depths of darkness. Picnickers would have boiled their kettles in the ruined room; lovers would have taken shelter there, lying on the bare floorboards; the shepherd would have kept his dinner on the bricks, and the tramp would have slept there wrapped in his coat against the cold. Later the roof would have caved in. Briars and hemlock would have smothered path, step and window, growing unevenly but vigorously over the mound, until a trespasser who had strayed off his path could have guessed only from a red-hot poker lily among the nettles, or a fragment of china in the hemlock, that someone had lived here once; that there had once been a house.

Had the feather fallen, had it tipped the scale, the whole house would have plunged to the bottom and lain there on the sands of oblivion. But a force was at work—something not very conscious; something that leered, something that lurched; something with no inspiration to perform its task with dignified ritual or solemn chanting. Mrs. McNab groaned; Mrs. Bast creaked. They were old and stiff, and their legs ached. At last they arrived with their brooms and pails and set to work. Out of the blue, one of the young ladies had written: would Mrs. McNab see that the house was got ready? Would she see to this, and see to that—and all in a rush. They might be coming for the summer; they had left everything till the last minute; they expected to find things the way they had left them. Slowly, painfully, with broom and pail, mopping and scouring, Mrs. McNab and Mrs. Bast held off the decay and the rot. They snatched things back from the pool of Time that was quickly closing over them—a basin here, a cupboard there. One morning they dragged up out of oblivion all of Scott’s Waverley novels and a tea service; in the afternoon they brought a brass fender and a set of steel fire irons back into the sun and air. George, Mrs. Bast’s son, trapped the rats and mowed the grass. They had the builders in. To the creak of hinges and the shriek of bolts, and the slamming and banging of woodwork swollen with damp, some rusty, toilsome birth seemed to be under way, as the women bent and straightened, groaned and sang, slapping and slamming about, up the stairs one moment and down in the cellars the next. Oh, the work of it, they said!

Some days they had their tea in the bedroom, or in the study, stopping work at midday with their faces smudged and their old hands stiff and cramped from gripping the brooms. Slumped in their chairs, they looked over their achievements: at one moment the splendid conquest of the taps and the bath; at another the harder and less complete victory over the long rows of books, once black as ravens, now blotched with white, growing pale mushrooms and hiding secretive spiders. Once again, as the tea warmed her inside, the telescope settled itself over Mrs. McNab’s eyes, and in a ring of light she saw the old gentleman on the lawn, thin as a rake, wagging his head and talking to himself, she supposed, as she came up with the washing. He never took any notice of her. Some said he was dead; others said it was her that was dead. Which was it? Mrs. Bast couldn’t say for sure either. The young gentleman was dead. That she did know. She had seen his name in the papers.

Then there was the cook—Mildred, Marian, some name of that kind—a red-haired woman, with a quick temper, as they all have, but kind as well, if you knew how to take her. Many’s the laugh they’d had together. She always kept back a plate of soup for Maggie—Mrs. McNab herself; sometimes a bit of ham; whatever was going spare. They lived well, back then. They had everything they wanted. (Sitting in the wicker armchair by the nursery fender, with the hot tea inside her, she unwound her ball of memories, easily and merrily.) There was always something going on—people in the house, twenty to stay at a time, sometimes, and washing up going on till well after midnight.

Mrs. Bast had never known the family; she had been living in Glasgow in those days. Setting down her cup, she wondered what on earth they had hung that animal’s skull up there for. Shot abroad somewhere, no doubt.

Very likely, said Mrs. McNab, letting her memories run on as they pleased. They had friends out in eastern countries; there were gentlemen staying, ladies in evening dress; once she had seen them all through the dining-room door, sitting at dinner. Twenty of them, she’d be bound, all in their jewels, and she was asked to stay on and help with the washing-up, till past midnight as like as not.

Ah, said Mrs. Bast, they’d find it changed. She leaned out of the window and watched her son George scything the grass. Well might they ask what had been done to it. Old Kennedy was meant to be looking after it, and then his leg got so bad after he fell off the cart; and after that, maybe nobody for a year, or most of one; and then Davie Macdonald; and seeds might have been sent, but who was to say whether they ever went in the ground? Oh, they’d find it changed.
She watched her boy at his scything. A great one for work, he was—one of your quiet sort. Well, she supposed they’d best get on with those cupboards. Up they hauled themselves.

At last, after days of hard work indoors and of cutting and digging outdoors, the dusters were given a final flick out of the windows, and the windows were closed; all over the house keys were turned; the front door slammed; the job was done.

And now, as though all the cleaning and scrubbing, the scything and mowing, had been drowning it out, there rose up that half-heard melody, that broken, fitful music that the ear half catches and then lets slip. A bark, a bleat—irregular, now and then, yet somehow connected. An insect humming, cut grass quivering—separate, yet somehow belonging together. A dor beetle’s drone, a wheel’s squeak, loud, soft, but mysteriously related. The ear strains to bring them together, and is always just about to make them into a harmony; but they are never quite heard, never fully harmonized, and at last, in the evening, the sounds die out one by one, the harmony wavers, and silence falls. As the sun set, the sharp edges faded, and quiet rose like a mist and spread; the wind dropped; the world shook itself loosely down to sleep—dark here, with no light in it except what filtered green through the leaves, or lay pale on the white flowers by the window.
[Late one evening in September, Lily Briscoe arrived and had her bag carried up to the house. Mr. Carmichael had come on the same train.]
